note: Hand-written copy for the Taiwan recommendations, keyed by slug. Edit this file, then run: pnpm tsx scripts/apply-recommendation-content.ts --country TW --apply

wang-s-broth.description: A Michelin Bib Gourmand stall inside Huaxi Street market that has been braising pork for over fifty years. The house bowl is lu rou fan — minced pork belly slow-cooked in soy, five-spice and rice wine, spooned over rice — and almost nothing on the menu costs more than a few dollars. Order at the counter, sit at a shared table, eat, leave. Cash only, and the lunch rush is genuinely busy.
highlights: Lu rou fan (braised pork rice) — the reason the stall has a Michelin mention
Add a bowl of the pork-and-radish soup; it cuts the richness
Bring cash and small notes, and expect to share a table
Go before noon or after 14:00 to skip the worst of the queue

fu-ba-wang-pig-s-knuckles.description: A Beiping-style specialist near Zhongxiao Xinsheng that sells one thing extremely well: braised pork knuckle, simmered until the skin turns to jelly and the meat falls off the bone. You pick a cut — the front leg is meatier, the back leg fattier — and it comes with rice and the braising liquid. Popular enough that they regularly sell out in the evening.
highlights: Ask for the front leg (前腔) if you want more meat, the back leg for more collagen
The braised bamboo shoots and pickled vegetables are the right side order
Go early — they close once the day's pork is gone
Takeaway boxes travel well if the queue is long

brasserie-regent-taipei.description: The buffet at the Regent Taipei, and one of the city's long-standing splurge meals. Seafood on ice, a sushi and sashimi counter, carved roasts, a Taiwanese section and a dessert room that is the real reason most people book. Sittings are timed and weekends sell out well in advance, so reserve.
highlights: Book ahead — weekend sittings go days in advance
Start at the seafood and sashimi counters; they are restocked least often at the end
Lunch sittings cost noticeably less than dinner for much the same spread
Leave room for the dessert room, which is the part people come back for

din-tai-fung-xinsheng-branch.description: The soup dumpling house that made Taiwanese food famous abroad, at its Xinsheng branch. Watch the kitchen through glass as the crew folds every xiao long bao to eighteen pleats, then eat them the proper way: into the spoon, nick the skin, drink the soup, then the dumpling with ginger and vinegar. Take a number at the door and expect to wait — the wait is part of it.
highlights: Classic pork xiao long bao first, then the crab roe version if you are splitting
Shrimp and pork shao mai, and the hong you chao shou (wontons in chilli oil)
Three parts vinegar to one part soy, plus a pile of shredded ginger
Take a queue ticket, then walk the block — they text when the table is ready
The stir-fried string beans and the wood ear salad reset the palate between rounds

shengyuan-xiao-long-bao.description: A neighbourhood soup-dumpling shop of the kind Taipei is full of and visitors rarely find: no queue system, no English menu, dumplings folded in front of you and steamed to order. The soup is lighter and the skins a touch thicker than at the famous chains, and a basket costs a fraction of the price.
highlights: Order by the basket and add a bowl of sour-and-spicy soup
Point at what the table next to you is having — the menu is Chinese only
A genuinely cheap alternative when the queue at the famous places is an hour
Cash is safest

hangzhou-xiao-long-bao.description: A long-running Taipei institution near Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, and the one locals name when they want to argue about soup dumplings without saying Din Tai Fung. Thin skins, a lot of soup, and a short menu of Jiangnan sides. Queues are real but move faster than at the tourist-famous branches.
highlights: Pork xiao long bao are the benchmark; the luffa-and-shrimp version is the local pick
Add the sweet taro dumplings at the end if they still have them
Walkable from Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, so pair the two
Put your name down, then wait outside — they call in Chinese and English

mingyue-tangbao.description: A small shop off Tonghua Street doing tang bao — the larger, soupier cousin of the xiao long bao, served with a straw so you can drink the broth before eating the skin. Worth it for the novelty and for the fact that it sits a minute from the Linjiang night market, so it works as a first course.
highlights: Drink the soup through the straw first, then eat the wrapper with vinegar
Pair it with a walk through Linjiang (Tonghua) night market next door
Small room, quick turnover — it is a stop, not a sit-down evening

iceeisbock.description: A tiny coffee bar built around one trick: the drink is frozen to around minus eighty and served as a shot in a cup of ice, so it stays cold and undiluted from first sip to last. The Eisbock-milk versions are the signature. It is a stand-and-drink place rather than somewhere to sit and work.
highlights: The Eisbock milk coffee is the signature — order that before anything else
Drink it where you buy it; the whole point is the temperature
Counter space only, so plan a few minutes rather than an afternoon

ice-eisbock-wu-space.description: The same sub-zero coffee concept inside Wu Space, a shared creative building — more room to sit than the original counter, and worth combining with whatever the building has on. Same frozen shots, same Eisbock milk base.
highlights: More seating than the original branch if you want to linger
Check what is showing in the building before you go — the space hosts rotating events
Same signature frozen Eisbock coffee

zhongcheng-shandong-scallion-pancake.description: A Tianmu stall selling Shandong-style cong you bing: dough laminated with scallion and lard, slapped flat and fried on a griddle until the outside shatters and the inside pulls apart in layers. Add an egg and it becomes a full breakfast for pocket change.
highlights: Order it with an egg (加蛋) — it is the standard upgrade for a reason
Ask for chilli sauce and a little soy paste rather than one or the other
Morning and early afternoon only; it is a breakfast stall
Eat it immediately — it loses the crackle within minutes

tian-jin-scallion-pancake.description: The Yongkang Street scallion pancake stall that has had a queue since 2001. Theirs is the cong zhua bing style — shredded and fluffy rather than crisp and flat — and the menu is a grid of add-ons: egg, basil, cheese, ham, corn. Open from morning to late, and the line moves quickly.
highlights: Egg and basil is the combination most regulars order
Point at the board and hold up fingers; service is fast and wordless
It sits on Yongkang Street, so pair it with the mango shaved ice nearby
Open roughly 08:00–22:00 daily, so it fills any gap in the day

modern-toilet-restaurant.description: A themed restaurant in Ximending where you sit on toilets, eat from porcelain bowls shaped like fixtures and drink from miniature urinals. The food is ordinary Taiwanese-Western comfort cooking — curries, hot pots, shaved ice — and nobody comes for it. Come for the photographs and the fact that it has somehow survived for decades.
highlights: Go for the spectacle, not the cooking — set expectations accordingly
The soft-serve in a squat-toilet bowl is the photograph everybody takes
Very much a with-friends or with-kids stop
Ximending is at its best after dark, so make it an evening

yu-pin-yuan-iced-and-hot-tangyuan.description: A dessert shop specialising in tangyuan — glutinous rice balls with a sesame or peanut centre — served two ways: hot in a sweet ginger or peanut soup in winter, or cold over shaved ice in summer. Simple, cheap and open late, which makes it a good last stop after a night market.
highlights: Black sesame filling is the classic; peanut is the sweeter one
Hot in ginger soup when it is cold out, iced with peanut and taro when it is not
Open late — it works as a post-night-market dessert
One bowl is enough for two people after a big meal

yuan-fang-gua-bao.description: Gua bao done properly: a steamed folded bun holding braised pork belly, pickled mustard greens, crushed peanut and coriander. You choose how fatty a cut you want, which is the whole decision. A single bao is a snack, two are lunch.
highlights: Choose your cut — lean (瘦肉), fatty (肥肉) or mixed (維肉) for the balance
Say no to coriander at the counter if it is not for you
Pair with a bowl of the four-herb soup (四神湯) for the classic combination
Cash, quick queue, no seating to speak of

mozhuting-ranmian-honjia.description: A noodle bar built around crab roe — a bowl of dan dan-style dry noodles under a spoonful of rich orange roe paste, around 180 NTD. Small, modern and usually full at lunch. You mix it yourself at the table until every strand is coated.
highlights: The crab roe dry noodles are the dish; everything else is a side
Mix hard for a full minute before the first bite — it is a dry noodle, not a soup
Around 180 NTD a bowl, which is a lot here and still worth it
Small room; go off-peak or expect to wait

toriaezu-curry.description: Taiwan's first Bib Gourmand curry house, opened by a chef who came from a two-star kitchen. Japanese-style curry, cooked down for days, served over rice with a small number of toppings. The menu is short on purpose and the room is tiny.
highlights: The signature beef curry is what the Michelin mention is for
Add the soft-boiled egg — it changes the texture of the whole plate
Seats are few; arrive at opening or well after the lunch peak
Cash is the safe assumption

lao-shan-dong-homemade-noodles.description: A hole in the wall that has been pulling its own noodles since the 1950s, in the arcade near Ximen. Beef noodle soup in the clear-broth northern style rather than the dark braised one, plus cold sides from the counter. The kind of place that looks like nothing and has a queue of office workers at 12:15.
highlights: Clear-broth beef noodles (清燉) here rather than the braised red version
Pick two or three cold sides from the counter — cucumber, seaweed, dried tofu
Hand-pulled noodles, so ask for them wide if you like more chew
Lunch is packed; 11:30 or 14:00 is a different experience

iyoshi-cola.description: A craft cola bar making the syrup from scratch — spices, citrus peel, kola nut — and mixing it to order. Around 150 NTD a glass, served in a small room that treats a soft drink with the seriousness of a cocktail bar.
highlights: Order it straight first to taste the spice, then try it with milk or lemon
Around 150 NTD; bottles of the syrup make a genuinely good souvenir
A short stop rather than a sit-down — the room is small

coffee-dumbo.description: A retro cafe with yellow chairs, a nineties playlist and an apple americano that is the reason half the room is photographing their table. Comfortable enough to sit in for an hour, small enough that you may wait for a seat at the weekend.
highlights: The apple americano is the signature — it is a filter coffee with apple, and it works
The yellow chairs are the photograph; the window seats get the light
Weekday afternoons are calm, weekends mean a wait
Good laptop-free hour rather than a work cafe

master-of-tea.description: A tea shop that went viral for a rose tea with a very direct effect on the digestive system — it is sold, and drunk, as a joke as much as a drink. Treat it as a novelty stop and know what you are ordering before you order it.
highlights: The rose tea is the viral one, and the effect it is famous for is real
Maybe not the drink to have before a long train ride
Everything else on the board is an ordinary, decent tea shop menu

ba-ma-shui-le.description: A nineties-nostalgia cafe near Chifeng Street stocked with old consoles — Famicom, N64, PlayStation — that you play while you eat. Drinks and light food, low lighting, and a crowd that stays for hours. Best with two or more people.
highlights: Consoles are first come, first served — go early evening for a free screen
Better with a group; the whole thing is built around taking turns
Chifeng Street around it is full of small bars for afterwards
Check the opening days before you go; hours are not nine-to-five

imaya-burger.description: The first location outside Japan of a Fukuoka burger shop that has been a Nishi Park fixture for decades. The burger sits in an oval koppepan roll rather than a bun, which is what makes it theirs — softer, sweeter, and closer to a Japanese bakery than an American diner.
highlights: The classic beef burger in the koppepan roll is the one to order
Small kitchen — expect a wait at lunch even when the queue looks short
Takes well as a takeaway to eat in a nearby park

ningxia-night-market.description: A compact, food-first night market in Datong — one street, both sides, very little that is not edible. It is the market most food tours use because the stalls are old, the specialities are clear and you can eat your way down it in an hour. Less crowded and less souvenir-heavy than Shilin.
highlights: Oyster omelette, taro balls and the sesame-oil chicken soup are the staples here
Hu jiao bing (pepper bun) and the fried taro cake near the temple end
One street, so you can do the whole thing in an hour without a map
Cash, small notes, and come hungry rather than after dinner

linjiang-tonghua-night-market.description: Tonghua night market, a short walk from Taipei 101, where the crowd is half neighbourhood and half visitor. Long, narrow and loud, with a good mix of food stalls, clothes and games. A practical option if you are staying in Xinyi and do not want to cross the city.
highlights: Walkable from Taipei 101 and Xinyi, so it pairs with an evening there
Look for the pork ribs in medicinal broth and the grilled squid
Mixed food and shopping rather than food-only — good for a browse
Busiest after 19:00 on weekends

nanjichang-night-market.description: A neighbourhood night market in Zhongzheng with almost no visitors and a Michelin-listed stall or two hiding in it. Prices are what locals pay, the stalls are family-run, and nobody will hand you an English menu. The best argument for skipping the famous markets entirely.
highlights: Look for the sesame oil chicken, the pot stickers and the fried rice stalls with the longest local queues
Prices here are a third of what the tourist markets charge
Cash only in practice, and small notes help
Go on a weekday evening — it is a neighbourhood market, not an event

huaxi-street-night-market.description: The old Wanhua market, once known for snake meat and now a covered lane of long-running food stalls next to Longshan Temple. Faded, atmospheric and genuinely old Taipei, with the neighbouring Guangzhou Street market attached to it.
highlights: Pair it with Longshan Temple, which is one block away
Wang's Broth (braised pork rice) is inside — the Michelin Bib Gourmand stall
Covered arcade, so it is the market to pick when it rains
Wander into Guangzhou Street market next door for more stalls

raohe-night-market.description: A straight, lantern-lit street market that runs from the Ciyou Temple gate to the far end and back, and the one most residents recommend over Shilin. The pepper buns at the temple entrance — pork and spring onion baked on the wall of a clay oven — have their own queue before the market even opens.
highlights: Hu jiao bing (black pepper bun) at the temple-gate stall — join the queue, it moves
Medicinal pork rib soup, stinky tofu, and the taro-ball dessert at the far end
Enter at the Ciyou Temple arch and walk one side down, the other back
From Songshan station, which is directly underneath
Better food and fewer stalls selling phone cases than Shilin

shilin-night-market.description: Taipei's biggest and most famous night market: a street level of clothes, games and souvenir stalls over a basement food court. Enormous, crowded and more commercial than the others, which is either the appeal or the reason to pick a different one.
highlights: The food is mostly in the basement food court, not at street level
Giant fried chicken cutlet, oyster omelette and the cheese potato are the classics
Go on a weekday if you can — weekends are shoulder-to-shoulder
If you only have one night market in you, Raohe or Ningxia is the better pick

elephant-mountain-xiangshan.description: A twenty-minute stair climb from the MRT that ends with the classic view of Taipei 101 rising out of the city. The stairs are steep and continuous, there is no shade, and it is worth every step around an hour before sunset when the tower lights come on against a blue sky.
highlights: Start about an hour before sunset and stay for the blue hour — that is the photograph
It is stairs the whole way; take water, and expect to sweat year-round
The first platform is crowded — keep climbing to the boulders for space
Xiangshan MRT, exit 2, then follow the signs; free, and open at night
A head torch makes the walk back down much easier

taipei-101.description: The tower that defined the skyline for a decade, with an observatory on floors 88 to 91 and one of the world's fastest lifts getting you there. The indoor deck has the tuned mass damper — a 660-tonne steel ball that keeps the building still in a typhoon — and the outdoor deck opens when the weather allows.
highlights: Book a timed slot online; the walk-up queue at sunset is the long one
The damper on 88 is the part people remember more than the view
Skyline Skyline 460 (the roof walk) is a separate, pricier ticket
Many locals will tell you Elephant Mountain is the better view for free — do both

longshan-temple-lungshan-temple.description: Taipei's most atmospheric temple, founded in 1738 and rebuilt after wartime bombing. Buddhist and Taoist deities share the same courtyards, incense is constant, and there is almost always a service being chanted. The Yue Lao shrine at the back is where people come to ask about love.
highlights: Try the moon blocks (擲筊) — two red crescents, dropped to ask a yes-or-no question
Come at dusk when the lanterns are lit and evening chanting starts
Enter by the dragon door on the right, leave by the tiger door on the left
Huaxi Street night market is one block away for dinner afterwards
Free, and modest dress is appreciated rather than enforced

chiang-kai-shek-memorial-hall.description: The white hall with the blue octagonal roof at the head of Liberty Square, flanked by the National Theater and Concert Hall. The changing of the honour guard happens on the hour and is the reason most people time their visit; the square itself is where Taipei holds its protests and its festivals.
highlights: Changing of the guard on the hour — arrive five minutes early for a front spot
The exhibition downstairs covers the history, including the contested parts
Liberty Square is at its best early morning or after dark, when it is lit
Free entry; CKS Memorial Hall MRT comes up inside the grounds

ximending.description: Taipei's pedestrian entertainment district — neon, street performers, cinemas, cheap clothes and a dense knot of street food. It is the loud, young part of the city and it works best after dark. The red-brick Red House theatre at the edge anchors the area's bar street.
highlights: Go after dark; in daylight it is just a shopping street
Ay-Chung flour-rice noodle is the famous standing-only bowl here
The Red House and the bar street behind it for a drink afterwards
Wall-to-wall on Friday and Saturday nights

dadaocheng.description: The nineteenth-century tea-trading quarter on the Tamsui river, now a mix of restored shophouses, old dried-goods merchants and small design shops. The wharf at the end has a row of container bars and one of the best sunsets in the city.
highlights: Walk Dihua Street first, then finish at Dadaocheng Wharf for sunset
The wharf's container bars are open in the evening from spring to autumn
Xia-Hai City God Temple mid-street is small and worth the two minutes
Best in late afternoon, when the shops are still open and the light is low

dihua-street.description: The spine of Dadaocheng: a street of nineteenth-century shophouses selling dried seafood, herbs, tea and fabric, with newer design studios and cafes filling the upper floors. It is at its most alive in the weeks before Lunar New Year, when the whole street becomes a market.
highlights: Buy dried mango, mushrooms or tea here rather than at an airport shop
Look up — the facades are the reason the street is protected
The Lunar New Year market in the two weeks before the holiday is the peak
Several of the restored houses have cafes hidden in the back courtyard

xinyi-district.description: The planned downtown around Taipei 101: department stores, skybridges, the city's biggest cinemas and the bar and club strip. Clean, modern and the least characteristically Taipei part of Taipei, which is exactly why it is a useful base.
highlights: The elevated walkways connect most of the malls without ever going outside
Tonghua night market is a ten-minute walk and far better value than the mall food halls
Xiangshan trailhead is one MRT stop away for sunset
Sunday afternoons are the busiest the district gets

tamsui-danshui.description: The end of the red MRT line, where the river meets the sea. An old-town waterfront of food stalls and street performers, a Spanish-then-Dutch fort on the hill, and a sunset that the whole city comes north for. Half a day, easily done on the metro.
highlights: Time the trip so you are on the waterfront for sunset — that is the point
A-gei (stuffed fried tofu) and iron eggs are the local specialities
Fort San Domingo and the old British consulate are a short uphill walk
Take the ferry across to Bali for the bike path and the other view back
Around 40 minutes from Taipei Main on the red line

taipei-performing-arts-center.description: The OMA-designed theatre in Shilin — a grey cube with a sphere embedded in one side, which is the auditorium. There is a public loop that walks you through the building's guts even without a ticket, and the plaza hosts large-scale street performance and festivals.
highlights: The public circulation loop is free and is the architectural tour
Check the programme before you go — the plaza events are the main draw
Directly above Jiantan MRT, which is also the Shilin night market stop
Worth it for the building alone if you care about architecture

rixing-type-foundry-approx.description: Very possibly the last traditional Chinese movable-type foundry in the world, kept running in a narrow Taipei workshop lined floor to ceiling with lead character blocks. You can visit, buy individual characters, and watch a craft that has essentially no successors.
highlights: Buy a few characters that mean something to you — they are sold individually
Small working shop, not a museum: go quietly and ask before photographing
Check opening hours in advance; it keeps workshop rather than tourist hours
Combine with Dadaocheng, which is a short walk away

c-lab-dome-theater.description: Taiwan's only immersive dome theatre, inside the C-LAB contemporary culture park on the old air force compound. Entry is free, the programme rotates, and the surrounding campus is a good wander of exhibition halls and lawns in its own right.
highlights: Free entry, but sessions are timed — check the schedule before crossing town
The wider C-LAB campus usually has two or three exhibitions on at once
Closed on Mondays, like most Taipei venues
Good rainy-day option near Da'an

xiangshan-six-boulders-observation-deck.description: The cluster of large rocks a little past the first Elephant Mountain platform, and the spot the skyline photographs actually come from. You climb onto a boulder, frame Taipei 101 between the trees, and wait your turn — there is a queue at sunset, and it is orderly.
highlights: Keep climbing past the crowded first platform — this is five minutes further
There is a polite queue for the best boulder at sunset; budget for it
A wide lens and a phone tripod earn their place here
Free, and lit enough to come back down after dark

national-taiwan-museum.description: The island's oldest museum, in a 1915 colonial hall at the top of 228 Peace Park — natural history, indigenous culture and Taiwan's own story. Small enough for an hour, and the building and the park around it are as much of the visit as the collection.
highlights: The indigenous peoples gallery is the strongest part of the collection
The building itself — dome, columns, stained glass — is the photograph
228 Peace Park around it is worth the walk through
Cheap ticket, closed Mondays

taipei-fine-arts-museum.description: Taipei's main contemporary art museum, in a stacked white modernist building beside the Yuanshan flower market. Large rotating shows, a strong Taiwanese contemporary collection, and enough space to spend a wet afternoon in.
highlights: Check what is on — the building is mostly given over to temporary shows
Saturday evenings are free entry
Closed Mondays; the Expo Park and flower market next door fill any gap
One of the better rainy-day options in the city

national-palace-museum.description: The world's great collection of Chinese imperial art, moved to Taipei in 1949 and rotated a few thousand pieces at a time. Bronzes, calligraphy, jade and porcelain spanning millennia — including the jadeite cabbage and the meat-shaped stone, which draw their own queues.
highlights: Go at opening or after 15:00; the tour-group crush is late morning
The jadeite cabbage and the meat-shaped stone are small, famous and crowded — see them first
Rent the audio guide, or the bronzes floor will pass you by
It is out in Shilin — allow travel time on top of the visit
Half a day is realistic; a full day is possible

wan-nian-commercial-building.description: A time-capsule shopping block in Ximending: several floors of tiny shops selling toys, models, retro games and odds and ends, in a building that has not been redecorated since the seventies. Half the appeal is the stairwells and the lighting.
highlights: Work upwards floor by floor — the best shops are not on the ground floor
Model kits, retro games and figures are what it is known for
The interior is the photograph: strip lights, tiled floors, narrow stairs
Open into the evening, like the rest of Ximending

binjiang-market.description: A working neighbourhood market rather than a sight — morning produce, butchers, prepared food — and a good place to photograph everyday Taipei without a single tour group in frame. Go early, buy something, be polite with the camera.
highlights: Morning only; by early afternoon most stalls have packed up
Buy fruit or a breakfast item rather than only photographing people at work
Ask before pointing a camera at a stallholder — it is usually a yes
Cash, small notes

qiyan-metro-station.description: An elevated station on the red line north of the city whose geometry — long curved canopy, repeating columns, strong shadows — has made it a photography stop. Nothing to do here but shoot, so combine it with Beitou or Tamsui further up the line.
highlights: Strong side light early morning or late afternoon makes the columns
Shoot from the platform ends, and stay behind the yellow line
Combine it with Beitou hot springs or Tamsui, both on the same line
Five minutes of shooting, not a destination on its own

songshan-ciyou-temple.description: The six-storey Mazu temple that forms the gateway to Raohe night market — gold, red and heavily carved, with lanterns that photograph beautifully against the market lights. Active rather than preserved: there is usually something being offered or chanted.
highlights: It is the Raohe market gate, so do both in one evening
Blue hour, with the lanterns lit and the market glow behind, is the shot
Upper floors are open and almost always empty
Free; keep to the side during services

yonghe-baofu-temple.description: A neighbourhood temple in Yonghe, across the river from Taipei — quiet, ornate and almost entirely free of visitors, which is what makes it good to photograph. A stop to fold into a walk rather than a trip in itself.
highlights: Empty compared with Longshan, so you can take your time
Roof ridge dragons and the carved stone columns are the detail worth shooting
Pair it with a wander through Yonghe, which is where the soy milk breakfast shops are
Free, active temple — be unobtrusive during services

sanchong-xianse-temple.description: A designated historic monument in Sanchong, dedicated to the god of agriculture and one of the oldest temples in the Taipei basin. Restored woodwork, painted beams, and the kind of stillness the famous temples no longer have.
highlights: A protected historic monument — the restoration work is the reason to look up
Almost never busy, so a good hour for photography
Across the river from Taipei; easiest on the orange line
Free entry

zhongshan-district.description: The neighbourhood between Taipei Main and the Songshan line: Japanese-era side streets, independent bookshops, coffee roasters and small boutiques, with Chifeng Street at its centre. Less spectacular and more livable than the tourist districts, and the best afternoon wander in the city.
highlights: Start at Chifeng Street and let the side lanes take you
Several of Taipei's best small coffee roasters are within four blocks
The Japanese-era buildings around Zhongshan MRT are worth the detour
Evening turns the same streets into small bars and wine shops

vintage-toy-shopping-plaza-zhongshan.description: A retro toy plaza where many of the shops are unmanned — you pick what you want and pay into a box or by QR code. Gashapon, model kits, second-hand figures and a lot of things that have not been made for thirty years.
highlights: Several stalls are unstaffed: take what you want and pay by the posted QR code
Bring coins for the gashapon machines
Prices are marked, so there is nothing to haggle over
Weekday afternoons are quietest

pokemon-themed-7-eleven.description: A fully Pokémon-branded convenience store — exclusive merchandise, themed shelving, a Pikachu you can be photographed with, and otherwise everything a normal 7-Eleven has. A short, cheap, genuinely fun stop if that is your thing.
highlights: The exclusive merchandise sells out; go early in the week after a restock
There is a photo spot inside, and a queue for it at weekends
Everything else is a normal 7-Eleven, so it doubles as a drinks stop
Ten minutes, not an outing

free-souvenir-stamps-mrt-museums.description: Taiwan keeps commemorative rubber stamps at train stations, MRT stations, museums, visitor centres and tourist sites — each one designed for that place, and all free. Carry a small notebook and the whole trip becomes a collecting game.
highlights: Buy a small blank notebook on day one — that is the whole kit
Railway stations, MRT information desks, museums and national park visitor centres
Shifen, Jiufen and most of the old streets have their own designs
Free everywhere; ask at the information desk if you cannot see the stand

wan-nian-building-toy-store.description: A retro toy shop inside the Wan Nian building in Ximending, stacked with old figures, models and souvenirs that nobody else still sells. Good for an unusual present and for the sheer density of the shelves.
highlights: Inside the Wan Nian building — work through the other floors while you are there
Old figures and models rather than current releases
Prices are marked; cash is easiest
Open into the evening with the rest of Ximending

scrumps-and-mushrooms-24hr-movie-theatre.description: A 24-hour private cinema where you book a room with a sofa, pick a film and have food brought to you. Genuinely useful for a late arrival, an early flight, or a rainy night with nothing else open.
highlights: Open around the clock — a real option for a red-eye layover
Rooms are private and booked by the hour; reserve at weekends
Food and drinks are delivered to the room rather than collected
Bring a jumper; the rooms run cold

capybara-knight-cafe.description: A capybara cafe — you buy a slot, wash your hands, and sit with the animals while they eat and, mostly, ignore you. Sessions are timed and capped, so booking matters. Whether it is for you depends on how you feel about animal cafes.
highlights: Book a timed slot online; walk-ins are often turned away
Buy the vegetable plate — it is the only way the capybaras will come to you
Sessions run about an hour and the room is small
Quieter on weekday mornings, when the animals are also more awake

bu-lao-song-massage.description: A reliable massage chain with branches across Taipei, easy to book the same day and priced by the half hour. Foot massage, full body, or the combination — a practical thing to schedule after a day of stairs and night markets rather than a spa experience.
highlights: Foot massage for 40 minutes is the standard after a walking day
Multiple branches, so book whichever is near where you are sleeping
Same-day booking is usually possible, even in the evening
Say early if the pressure is too much — the default is firm

major-league-batting-field.description: Indoor batting cages in Ximending, coin-operated and open late. Baseball is the national sport here and this is the cheapest way to take part in it for twenty minutes between dinner and a bar.
highlights: Coin-operated — bring change, or get it at the counter
Cages are graded by pitch speed; start slower than you think
Helmets and bats are provided
Open late, so it works as a post-dinner detour in Ximending

ye-sen-animal-school.description: A hands-on animal park in Neimen, Kaohsiung, where the visit is structured as guided interaction — foxes, eagles, ponies and others — rather than walking past enclosures. Open 10:00 to 17:00 and closed on Wednesdays.
highlights: Open 10:00–17:00, closed Wednesdays — check before making the drive
Sessions are guided, so arriving early in the day gets you more of them
Well outside Kaohsiung city; a car or scooter makes it far easier
Wear shoes and clothes you do not mind getting muddy

kun-s-crystal-diy-glass-blowing.description: A glass studio where you make the thing yourself — a blown piece or a small jewellery item — with a maker guiding your hands. Sessions are short, the result is yours to take, and it is one of the better rainy-afternoon options in Taipei.
highlights: Book ahead; sessions run to a schedule and are capped
Blown pieces need cooling time, so allow for collection or ask about posting
Tie long hair back and wear closed shoes — there is an actual furnace
Works well for two people; less so for a large group

retro-jam-print-studio.description: A Japanese-founded silkscreen and risograph studio where you can walk in and print your own zine, poster or postcards. The risograph colours — fluorescent pink, blue, yellow — are the point, and staff will walk a beginner through a first print.
highlights: Bring artwork on a USB stick or your phone to save studio time
Risograph fluorescents do not exist in normal printing — use them
Book the press rather than turning up, especially at weekends
A finished stack of prints is a better souvenir than anything in a gift shop

custom-pet-portrait-street-artist.description: A street artist who draws a custom portrait of your pet from a photo, for around 350 TWD and roughly two hours of work. You hand over the photo, go and do something else, and come back for it.
highlights: Around 350 TWD, and about two hours — drop off and come back
Bring a clear, well-lit photo; it is the whole input
Cash
Plan something nearby for the wait rather than standing around

go-shrimping-hejiang-st.description: Taiwanese shrimping: you rent a rod, sit at the edge of an indoor pool with a beer, catch freshwater prawns, and grill what you catch at the table. Deeply local, mildly absurd, and an entire evening once you get into it.
highlights: Rods are rented by the hour — two hours is the usual first booking
Salt your catch heavily before grilling; that is the house method
Open very late, and the crowd gets more fun after 22:00
You will catch nothing for the first half hour. Everybody does.

186-roller-skating.description: An indoor roller rink on Civic Boulevard — skate hire, a mixed crowd of regulars and beginners, and music loud enough that nobody is watching you fall over. A cheap, unusual evening.
highlights: Skate hire is on site; socks are the only thing worth bringing
Evening sessions are busier and more fun than afternoons
Regulars skate the inside lane — beginners keep to the outside
Cheap by the session

xiang-diao-diao-shrimp-fishing.description: A 24-hour shrimp and lobster fishing hall in Taoyuan, close enough to the airport to be the standard answer for a long layover. Rent a rod, fish, grill, eat, sleep on the plane.
highlights: Open 24 hours — the reason it works for an overnight airport layover
Lobster pools cost more per hour than the shrimp pools but bite faster
They will grill your catch for you if you ask
Taoyuan, not Taipei — close to the airport, far from the city

babylon-club.description: A Taipei nightclub — late opening, guest DJs, and a door that gets selective after midnight at weekends. Check who is playing before committing an evening to it.
highlights: Nothing happens before midnight; arriving at 23:00 means an empty room
Check the line-up — the crowd changes completely with the booking
Bring photo ID; it is checked
Table service is the norm for larger groups

wave-club.description: A club in the Xinyi nightlife strip, mainstream in booking and busy at weekends. Convenient if you are already in Xinyi and want the night to keep going.
highlights: In the Xinyi strip, so easy to combine with dinner nearby
Weekends are the point; weeknights are quiet
Dress code is enforced loosely but it is enforced
Fills after midnight

fake-sober-bar.description: A cocktail bar rather than a club — smaller room, proper drinks, conversation possible. The kind of place to end an evening instead of starting one.
highlights: Ask the bartender for something off-menu; that is where the good drinks are
Small room, so a reservation helps at weekends
Better as a nightcap than as the whole evening

sun-moon-lake.description: Taiwan's largest lake, ringed by a 33 km cycle path that regularly appears on lists of the world's most scenic. Bikes rent for around 150 TWD a day, there are temples and a gondola on the shore, and the morning mist off the water is the reason to stay overnight rather than day-trip it.
highlights: Rent a bike (around 150 TWD/day) and ride at least the Shuishe–Xiangshan section
The full 33 km loop includes road sections; the dedicated path is the scenic half
Take the ropeway up for the view over the lake and the Formosan village
Reached via Taichung — HSR to Taichung, then the bus to Shuishe
Stay a night: the early-morning mist is what people come back for

alishan-forest-railway-national-forest.description: A narrow-gauge mountain railway that climbs from Chiayi through Fenqihu to the Alishan forest, and one of the great train rides in Asia. Up top: cedar trails, a sunrise train to Zhushan, and the Mianyue line, which walks you through disused rail tunnels.
highlights: Book the forest railway well ahead — seats sell out, especially at weekends
Fenqihu is the classic mid-way stop, and its railway bento is part of the ritual
The sunrise train to Zhushan leaves before dawn; buy the ticket the night before
The Mianyue trail runs through old rail tunnels and is the quiet alternative to the main paths
It is cold and wet up there year-round — bring layers and a rain shell

teapot-mountain.description: A short, steep hike from the Jinguashi Gold Museum up to a teapot-shaped rock, with the Yin-Yang Sea — where mineral run-off turns the bay two colours — below you the whole way. Around two hours return, and far less crowded than Jiufen down the hill.
highlights: Start from the Gold Museum in Jinguashi; the trail is signposted from there
About two hours return, steep, with ropes and a scramble near the summit
The Yin-Yang Sea view is best on a clear morning before the cloud comes in
Combine with Jiufen, which is fifteen minutes away by bus
No shade and no water on the trail

jiufen-old-street.description: A former gold-mining town stacked up a mountainside above the sea, with a lantern-lit stair street of tea houses and food stalls at its centre. It is crowded by mid-morning and magical for the twenty minutes after the lanterns come on, which is the argument for staying past sunset.
highlights: Stay for dusk — the lanterns lit against a blue sky is the photograph everybody comes for
Sit down in a tea house on the A-Mei terrace side for the view over the bay
Taro balls, peanut ice-cream rolls with coriander, and the fish-ball soup
Day-trippers arrive 10:00–16:00; before or after that it is a different town
Bus from Ruifang station, or the direct bus from Taipei — the last one back leaves earlier than you think

shifen.description: An old railway street where the track runs between the shopfronts and everybody releases a paper sky lantern from the sleepers between trains. Ten minutes away is Shifen Waterfall, the widest in Taiwan. Touristy, unapologetically, and still worth doing once.
highlights: Write on all four sides of the lantern — each colour stands for a different wish
The shop photographs the release for you; hand over your phone before you light it
Walk the ten minutes to Shifen Waterfall, which most lantern visitors skip
On the Pingxi branch line — buy the one-day pass and hop between Shifen, Jingtong and Houtong
There is a souvenir stamp station at the station

yeh-liu-geopark.description: A north-coast headland of wind- and sea-carved sandstone, most famously the Queen's Head, a mushroom rock with a neck that erodes a little thinner every year. A boardwalk loop takes about an hour, and there is no shade anywhere on it.
highlights: Go early — the Queen's Head has a roped queue by mid-morning
The far end of the headland is nearly empty and geologically the best part
No shade at all: hat, water, sunscreen, and avoid the middle of the day in summer
Combine it with Jiufen or Keelung on a north-coast day
Closes in bad weather, so check before travelling

matsu-islands.description: A scattered archipelago far closer to China than to Taiwan — granite villages, decommissioned military tunnels cut into cliffs, and, in the right months, the bioluminescent plankton locals call blue tears. Reached by plane or overnight ferry, and weather cancels both.
highlights: Blue tears are seasonal — roughly April to September, best on a moonless night
Beihai Tunnel by boat is the single best thing on the islands
Flights are cancelled by fog regularly; build slack into the itinerary
Scooter rental is how everybody gets around — bring a licence that is accepted
Qinbi village on Beigan is the stone-house one worth an overnight

shanhu-beike-temple.description: A temple built entirely from shells and coral — millions of them, pressed into walls, columns and grottoes until the interior looks like a cave. There is nothing else like it, and it is small enough to see in half an hour.
highlights: The grotto passages at the back are the part worth the trip
Small — half an hour covers it, so pair it with something else nearby
Awkward to reach on public transport; a car or taxi makes sense
Free, and an active temple rather than an attraction

zhengbin-fishing-harbor.description: A working Keelung harbour whose row of terraced houses was painted in blocks of colour, giving Taiwan its most photographed waterfront. Best in late afternoon when the light hits the facades and the reflections settle.
highlights: Shoot from the opposite quay — the whole colour row and its reflection only line up from there
Late afternoon light, calm water; midday flattens it
Keelung's Miaokou night market is fifteen minutes away for dinner
Still a working harbour, so keep clear of the boats and the ramps

bitoujiao-trail.description: A coastal ridge walk on the northeast cape, out to a lighthouse, with cliffs dropping into the sea on both sides. Around two hours return, exposed the whole way, and one of the best walks within day-trip range of Taipei.
highlights: Two hours return to the lighthouse and back along the ridge
Completely exposed — wind, sun and no shelter; check the forecast
Best on a clear day; in haze the coastline disappears and so does the point
Bus from Ruifang, so it combines with Jiufen or the Pingxi line

houtong-cat-village.description: A former coal-mining village on the Pingxi line that emptied out and then filled up again with cats — several hundred of them, cared for by residents and volunteers, wandering a hillside of old mine buildings and cafes.
highlights: Buy cat food in the village rather than bringing your own — the residents ask for it
The coal-mining museum and the old bridge are genuinely interesting beyond the cats
Do not pick the cats up; they are free-roaming residents, not exhibits
On the Pingxi line, so it pairs with Shifen on the same one-day pass
Weekday mornings are quiet; weekends are a crowd

tainan.description: Taiwan's oldest city and the one people travel for the food: beef soup at breakfast, danzai noodles, coffin bread, shrimp rolls. Add four centuries of temples, a Dutch fort, and a pace noticeably slower than Taipei's. Two hours from Taipei by high-speed rail.
highlights: Beef soup for breakfast — the meat is sliced raw and cooked by the broth at the table
Danzai noodles, coffin bread, milkfish congee and shrimp rolls are the shortlist
Chihkan Tower, Anping Fort and the tree house at Anping for the history half
Two hours on the HSR from Taipei; a full weekend is the right amount
Most famous food stalls close by mid-afternoon — eat early

taichung.description: Taiwan's second city and the usual staging post for Sun Moon Lake and Alishan. Worth a stop for the Rainbow Village, the Miyahara ice-cream hall, a strong cafe scene and Fengjia, the largest night market on the island.
highlights: Fengjia night market is the biggest in Taiwan — go hungry
Miyahara: an old ophthalmology clinic turned ice-cream and gift hall
The National Taichung Theater by Toyo Ito is worth twenty minutes for the building
The natural base for Sun Moon Lake, an hour and a half away by bus
Bubble tea was invented here, and the original shops still trade on it

crown-coast-north-coast-corridor.description: The north-coast corridor between Keelung and the cape: the painted harbour at Zhengbin, sea-carved rock at Yehliu, the Elephant Trunk rock at Shenao, and a retired coal railway you now pedal along on a rail bike. A full day with a car, a stretched one without.
highlights: The Shenao rail bike runs on the old coal line along the coast — book a slot
Zhengbin harbour, Yehliu's rock formations and Elephant Trunk Rock in one loop
Far easier with a car or scooter; buses link the sights but slowly
Windy and exposed in winter — a spring or autumn day is the good one

crocodile-island-possibly-turtle-guishan.description: Almost certainly Guishan (Turtle) Island off Yilan — a volcanic island shaped like a swimming turtle, with milky turquoise sulphur vents in the sea around it. Landings are capped by permit and boats only run in season and in good weather; most trips are a circuit with whale and dolphin watching.
highlights: Landing permits are limited and released in advance — book through a Wushi Harbour operator
Boats run roughly March to November and are cancelled for swell
The 401 steps to the summit need a separate permit again, and start early
Whale and dolphin sightings are common on the crossing
Wushi Harbour in Yilan is the departure point, around 90 minutes from Taipei
